Health watchdog

The watchdog: gateway health verdicts, alert pushes, scheduled runs, and the compatibility smoke.

About 13 min read · 7 sections

On this page
01 What it checks 02 What is wrong now 03 The compatibility smoke 04 Serving-host execution probe 05 State file 06 The alert push 07 Schedule

gateway health answers one question for a single Mac: did the ChatGPT app move under the gateway, and did anything break when it did? It runs entirely on the local machine. The only network calls are the loopback inference probe and, with --push, the one heartbeat to the alert monitor. The compatibility smoke adds none of its own: its mock upstream is on loopback, and its engine config sets features.plugins = false, which stops the app engine from cloning github.com/openai/plugins into its private home (checked against engine 0.163: without the key git ls-remote and git fetch run within seconds of start, with it none do).

gateway health [--json] [--push] [--smoke]

Exit codes: 0 is ok, 1 is warn, 2 is fail (and the same 2 means the monitor URL was refused or no gateway configuration could be read), and 3 means the verdict was computed but the monitor never took it. --json prints the same verdict as one machine-readable object.

What it checks

Section Question Verdict moves
app The bundled Codex engine (--version of the signed CodexCLI.app binary) and the app's CFBundleShortVersionString, compared with the last pair seen. A change is recorded as info and triggers the smoke; a missing app is info, never a failure.
components gateway versions: every role still running an older release. A service still running any older release after one hour fails, including a patch update. Other components more than one minor behind for over 48 hours fail; a loaded chat engine can retain its original release. The clock starts when current was switched (the link's own mtime), not when the process started. A newer service during rollback does not count as older.
upgrade Why a service behind the installed release has not moved, from the service plan and the status snapshot. A service whose controllerRelease is the installed release moved live and is not lagging or stale; this adds the info "service moved live; its execution host follows once chats drain: see gateway activity". Otherwise, with a Claude Desktop component configured, the service refuses every automatic restart, so it never moves on its own: this warns "service upgrade blocked by Claude Desktop components: run gateway service restart --force when Claude is idle". Otherwise it adds the info "service upgrade waits for no running turn: see gateway activity". Since 1.5.2 a lagging service no longer refuses newer apps when both releases prepare engines identically (per-chat rollout).
service The unified service snapshot: component states, execution-host state, and host restarts in the last 15 minutes of telemetry. A failed host fails; a non-running component warns, except a paused native relay, which is info.
inference GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/health from the configured port. Anything not serving, a non-200 answer, or a release header that is not the installed one moves the verdict. A server that answers but holds back a change to gateway.json adds configRejected (one of rebind, restart_required, invalid, unreadable) to its answer, and the check warns "gateway.json change not applied (reason); fix it or restart the service" for as long as the file stays refused; any other value is ignored, see live configuration. clientOnly configs report the section as remote.
errors The local telemetry window (today's and yesterday's JSONL, fixed fields, counts only): session-method refusals, config retries followed by a refusal, and component exits. A refusal fails only when three or more are each under 5 minutes old and after the last recovery; a refusal that has stopped warns with the time it stopped (UTC). A config retry that still ends in an ongoing refusal fails; exits warn unless a restart explains them. See what is wrong now.
desktop The ChatGPT process tree, when <state>/desktop-registration.json names a wrapper. ChatGPT running on its stock engine warns; ChatGPT not running is info. See the stock engine.
smoke The packaged compatibility check against the installed release and the app's engine. A failing check fails; a check that cannot run warns.

Findings use a fixed vocabulary of phrases plus counts and versions. Reports never carry paths, command arguments, or error text. Anything that reaches one from outside — an X-Gateway-Release header, an inference body status, a phase name from the check or from the state file — has to look like a version token or a phase slug first, and is named unknown rather than quoted if it does not.

The service's optional runningRelease is frozen when that process starts. The watchdog uses it only when the status PID matches a live service row and the snapshot was published after that process started. It overrides a guessed inventory release: a signed app-owned Node does not necessarily map its loaded JavaScript, and a floating current command path can otherwise follow a new installation before the service actually moves. Missing, malformed, mismatched, or older status snapshots do not override the inventory.

A native relay whose binary is byte-identical to the installed release's is not lagging or stale. Releases reuse a built relay, so its release label can stay old with nothing to move to. gateway versions still prints that label, and gateway rollout counts it as retained. A relay with different bytes still warns.

A section that cannot be read says so once, as a warning (versions unreadable, telemetry unreadable, inference unreadable), and the rest of the run continues, push included. A watchdog that could not run ps is degraded, not broken, and it still has to answer.

What is wrong now

The watchdog reports what is wrong now, not what was wrong somewhere in the last 15 minutes. A Mac that healed itself must not page for the rest of the window, because --push turns a fail into a "down" on the alert monitor.

Refusals. A session refusal (rpc_error on thread/start, thread/resume, thread/fork or turn/start) is ongoing when at least one happened in the last 5 minutes and after the latest recovery marker. The markers are an execution_host_recovered event, a self_upgrade of the service or the server, and the start of the service process itself (read from the service row of gateway versions, since the service logs no start event). Two guards keep a marker from hiding a real outage: a recovered host is not a marker when an execution_host_failed or execution_host_restarted follows it, so a host that flaps cannot hold the verdict at warn; and the service's own start counts only once the service has been up for 5 minutes, so a service that crashes and restarts cannot keep resetting it. A refusal fails only when three or more are each under 5 minutes old and after the marker; fewer warn. A refusal that is no longer ongoing warns and says when it stopped: refused thread/resume 14x, none since 07:25 UTC. A config retry followed by a refusal fails only while the refusal is ongoing. Nothing about the counts in --json changes: errors.rpcErrors and errors.refusals still cover the whole window.

Exits a restart explains. A component_exit is not counted when it is within 15 seconds (either side) of a restart that explains it, matched by component:

Event near the exit Explains an exit of
self_upgrade of the service any component (the whole service restarts)
self_upgrade of the server inference
server_drain inference

An exit of the same kind far from any such event, or of a component the restart does not touch (a tunnel next to a server_drain), still warns. Without this every Mac warned inference exited 1x right after its own self-upgrade, which was the idle restart itself.

The stock engine

With an active desktop registration (the receipt has a wrapper) and ChatGPT running, the watchdog reads /bin/ps (pid, ppid and command only) through the same injectable command seam as the app check, and looks at ChatGPT's direct children:

Child of /Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/MacOS/ChatGPT Meaning
<install>/current/runtime/bin/node <install>/current/package/dist/cli.js codex-shim ... The app runs on the gateway. Nothing is reported.
.../CodexCLI.app/Contents/MacOS/codex ... app-server The app runs on its own engine. Warns: "ChatGPT started before the gateway (for example right after a reboot); quit and reopen ChatGPT to use gateway chats".
Codex (Service), Codex (Renderer), codex ... exec-server Ignored.

ChatGPT not running is reported as info (ChatGPT not running), and a Mac with no registration is not checked at all. No process's environment is ever read.

Verdict mapping

Situation Finding Verdict
3+ refusals, each under 5 minutes old and after the last marker refused <method> Nx fail (exit 2)
1-2 refusals under 5 minutes old and after the last marker refused <method> Nx warn (exit 1)
Refusals that stopped, or that a marker ended refused <method> Nx, none since HH:MM UTC warn
A newer adapter refused (release_skew_refused, adapter_newer) since the service last moved or started (a restart answers them); a live controller swap does not count chats refused Nx: the service still runs an older release ... fail (exit 2)
Exit explained by a restart none no change
Any other component exit <kind> exited Nx warn
Registered ChatGPT on the stock engine the sentence above warn
Registered, ChatGPT not running ChatGPT not running ok (info)

Exit codes are unchanged: 0 ok, 1 warn, 2 fail, 3 push not taken.

The compatibility smoke

When the app pair changes (or --smoke forces it), the watchdog runs scripts/e2e-fast-mode.mjs --gateway <installed bin> --package <package root> --codex <app engine> --transports stdio --root <private directory>. The child sees only PATH, HOME, TMPDIR and LANG, and its output is discarded apart from the last JSON line's failedPhase name on failure.

The check keeps its own state out of the real home. Every child it starts (the gateway, the executor host, the Codex shim and the engine) runs with HOME set to a private home folder (0700) inside its /tmp/gw-fast-* run folder, so the execution-host homes under ~/.local/state/gw-exec, the relay and SSH control homes (gw-native, gw-ssh) and the default ~/.codex all resolve inside the run folder and leave with it. The fixture still passes its own CODEX_HOME to the children that take one. The one path it cannot move is the pinned engine's socket folder, /tmp/codex-daemon-<uid>, which the engine fixes itself and the live gateway shares. When the run ends, the check removes there only the sockets and lock files whose names come from socket paths inside its own private home, and only when nothing is listening on them.

Stopping it is a sequence, not a signal. The check starts its gateway, executor and engine in process groups of their own, so after the 10-minute timeout the watchdog sends SIGTERM to the check's group and gives it 15 seconds to take its own children down; only a group that ignores the ask gets SIGKILL, and once the check has closed the group is swept with SIGKILL for anything it left behind. The check handles SIGTERM and SIGINT the same way it handles the end of its own run: its handlers are installed before it creates anything, it spawns nothing once teardown has begun, and it stops each child's whole process group (SIGTERM, three seconds, then SIGKILL, and a sweep after the child closes) until none is left, so the engine's own helpers and the /tmp/gw-fast-* folder leave with it. A failure names the step it stopped in (serve, catalog, stdio-host, stdio-open, stdio-catalog, or the check's own phases). Stopping the service aborts a check that is still running through the same sequence, which is why a shutdown does not wait for a ten-minute run.

The run folder lives under <state>/health/smoke-<timestamp> (0700) and is removed afterwards. The answer is stored against the app pair, so a quiet tick repeats the recorded answer instead of paying ten minutes again — including a recorded failure, which stays in every report for that pair until the app moves or --smoke runs the check again. A missing script or missing installed release reads as unavailable and warns.

Serving-host execution probe

Rollout readiness asks the running execution host for execution/probe. This is a real function-tool canary: it starts the release's verified gateway SDK in a private temporary home, uses only a loopback mock provider, and makes its disposable Git repository write a nonce-bearing file and local commit through exec_command. It never sends paid inference or reads the Mac's gateway configuration, credentials, chat history, hooks, plugins, MCP settings, or native home.

The host captures its PID/start identity, loaded release, source receipt, catalog fingerprint, and SDK checksum before it starts the child, then checks all of them again before returning success. A changed or unavailable identity, catalog, release, or SDK is never ready, even if the child completed. Calls coalesce while one canary is running; the run is bounded to 30 seconds and shutdown terminates only its private child process group.

The response uses fixed reason codes and only these proof booleans: sdkVerified, configVerified, directToolVerified, completedTurn, and commandVerified. It never includes command text, tool arguments, paths, environment values, provider responses, or child errors. Rollout readiness passes only when every proof is true and the identity remained unchanged.

State file

<state>/health-state.json (0600) holds exactly two records: the last app bundle/engine pair seen, and the last smoke answer with the pair it was earned against. Deleting it costs one re-run of the smoke; nothing else reads it.

The alert push

--push sends the verdict to one Uptime Kuma push monitor (which routes to Discord). The monitor URL lives only in <state>/alert-push-url. That file must be a regular file owned by the current user with no group or other permission bits (0600); anything wider is refused with exit 2 so a neighbour cannot read or flip the alert switch. The URL is never printed, logged, or repeated in an error: failures map to timeout, http_<status>, or network, and the watchdog sends one heartbeat per run rather than retrying in a loop.

The request is GET <url>?status=up|down&msg=<summary>&ping= with a 10-second timeout. The three keys are set on the URL that was read from the file, not appended to it: a URL pasted out of Uptime Kuma already ends in ?status=up&msg=OK&ping=, and a second copy of each would leave the monitor showing OK forever. ok and warn send up (the message names the warn), and only fail sends down. The message is gateway <verdict> plus as many finding phrases as 200 characters allow.

A file the watchdog will not read — wider than 0600, not a regular file, owned by someone else, a link, or a URL that is not http(s) with a host — is refused as insecure: the finding alert push url not private, the same words once on stderr, and exit 2. The alert path being broken is a failure even when the Mac itself is quiet, and neither message repeats the path or what was in it.

Schedule

The unified service supervisor calls startHealthSchedule from src/health-schedule.ts, which runs the health checks and their push in-process every 10 minutes: the first tick waits a full interval, ticks never overlap, and an unref'd timer keeps the service free to exit. The schedule stands down while alert-push-url does not exist, so a Mac without a monitor URL never pays for the checks. Its stop function also aborts the tick it started: a compatibility check that is still running is stopped, with its process group, rather than being left to finish. No LaunchAgent alternative is provided.
